results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 58 prose units align one-to-one, in order, with spec paragraphs p01-p57 (including p24a and p56); every outliner summary states the controlling idea of its aligned paragraph (e.g. Commute ¶8 'Commute volume arithmetic drives Hearthly's routing choice' = p47; Clustering ¶4 'Count canonical properties, not listings' = p24a). The five callouts match no spec paragraph, as expected.
The outliner marked no unit two_ideas; each summary names a single idea.

Every unit advances at least one of S1-S6 as the spec declares: the scene and map-product units S1, five-ways/architecture S2, clustering privacy and canonical-unit units S3, polygon and commute normalization S4, routing terms and arithmetic S5, performance and Chief Architect's View S6. Neighborhood rules (S2/S3) are the loosest link but stay tied to compiled filters and minimum counts.

Tables (five ways, map vs list, clustering, commute patterns, trade-offs, verticals) are each introduced and interpreted in adjacent prose; Figures 1-2 are referenced in text and Figures 3-5 sit next to the prose that describes what they show; quotations (Airbnb 80% and NDCG, Rightmove 'rich, map-centric results', TravelTime 'transactional model', Rightmove 8:48 pm) are each followed by what they show and their limits; the Hearthly statistics are used in the polygon replay, the arithmetic and the conclusion. One exception is recorded separately (Performance ¶1).

results.draft_locus: Performance and Caching at the Peak ¶1
results.quote: At Veldmark, an illustration, the group peak is about **31,000 queries per second** on Sunday evenings, 20:00–22:00 CET.
results.finding: The group peak figure is stated but never related to the map: the paragraph does not say what share of it is map traffic or why the group figure matters next to Hearthly's 2,700 of 4,200, and it is not used again (reader B item 7). The spec's 'shows' is that the map is the majority of Hearthly's peak load; the 31,000 figure is left unexplained.

All transition_in boundaries were read. Each opening sentence expresses its declared relationship: e.g. similarity ('[[recommendations]] showed ... the map is another such surface'), example ('Veldmark ... offers the case'), cause_effect ('Two consequences follow'), contrast ('Aggregations can leak what pins hide', 'The alternative is a self-hosted routing engine'), sequence with the question named ('which is Ingrid's second question', 'Ingrid's third question needs a second polygon'), emphasis ('The table hides one cross-cutting cost'), time ('What to watch over the long term'). Weakest boundaries (Five Ways and Architecture not naming Ingrid's first question; 'The five expressions meet buyers on the map'; review-block openers) still express sequence/problem-solution; the map-product bridge's thinness is recorded under flow.

Post level: both readers describe problem (scene with three questions) -> concepts (five ways, map as product) -> compiler -> its parts in turn -> worked example -> review block -> hand-off, and say the roadmap announces this order and the chapter keeps it. This agrees with the declared prerequisite_order with problem_solution and large_to_small. No top-level section is unclear to both; individual lost-thread points follow.

results.quote: So the map, like the recommendation surfaces, needs its own ranking and evaluation, built on content, availability and the contacts it leads to rather than on clicks, which reward what catches the eye rather than what a buyer pursues.
results.finding: The paragraph states the map-needs-its-own-ranking claim in its first sentence and again after the place-first argument, so both readers went back to check whether anything new was said. The spec says the claim is stated after the place-first argument; the opening sentence should carry over only recommendations' lesson.

results.quote: Part IV argues that most discovery queries are filters in disguise, and that the platform should compile a buyer's words, places and saved searches into its own structure; this chapter does that for place.
results.finding: Both readers could not tell whether this chapter belongs to Part IV or refers to it from outside; saying 'This part argues' (or naming the chapter that argues it) removes the doubt.

results.draft_locus: The Map Is a Different Product ¶1
results.quote: The five expressions meet buyers on the map.
results.finding: The section bridge is thin: it carries the five expressions over but does not introduce the spec's point that the map is not a list with pins, and the paragraph jumps straight to Airbnb's ranking evidence. Both readers had to work out what the section was for.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: A Geo Query Compiler in Front of the Engine ¶4
results.quote: A single pan, the most frequent interaction, shows the design at work: snapping the viewport to tiles makes it cacheable (Figure 2).
results.finding: Both readers found the 'A pan, a zoom, a count' subsection out of place (reader B: position 'unclear'; reader A: 'less clearly placed') and noted that its choices (tile snapping, approximate counts, separate side-list path) are restated as levers in Performance and Caching at the Peak ('Approximate counts and separate request paths for counts, clusters and the side list'). The repetition comes from the spec placing p20-p21 in the architecture section and listing the same items again as p41 levers; the spec should either move them to performance or make p41 refer back instead of re-listing.

results.draft_locus: Commute Search: Isochrones and Travel Times ¶2
results.quote: Behind both forms sit two patterns, which a platform will usually need together; My Places is per-listing travel time.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this sentence: 'both forms' and 'two patterns' sound like the same pair, the clause after the semicolon maps only one form to one pattern and repeats the previous paragraph, and the prose never names the two patterns (isochrone filter computed once and cached vs per-listing travel times by matrix call) that the spec's controlling idea states.

results.draft_locus: Commute Search: Isochrones and Travel Times ¶8
results.quote: If each matrix covers up to 50 pins (50 is the largest list page) and one or two of the user's places, that adds about 13,500 to 27,000 matrix elements per second.
results.finding: Both readers stopped at the premises of the arithmetic: reader A at the map calculation bounded by the list page size (and at the routing decision landing under the 'Caching isochrones' subheading), reader B at 'each needing an isochrone and a travel-time matrix for its pins', unsure whether every pan needs an isochrone. The order (arithmetic after the cache hit rate) is the spec's and sound; the prose should state the premises (one isochrone per parameter change, one matrix per page of pins on screen) and mark the decision as its own step.

results.draft_locus: Performance and Caching at the Peak ¶1
results.quote: Map requests are about 2,700 of Hearthly's 4,200 peak requests per second, because each session sends many of them.
results.finding: Both readers found this paragraph jump from the group peak to Rightmove to Hearthly without a clear point, with the Hearthly figure repeated from the scene and the group figure never related to it (reader A: 'without a clear point beyond "map traffic peaks too"').

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: The Lyon Apartment on the Map ¶2
results.quote: It is not a record of what happened: the team takes an evening session from May 2027, when the flat was listed, and runs it through the target design of Figure 1, including the commute search that does not exist yet.
results.finding: Both readers had to re-read to fit the timeline (September 2027 session, flat listed in May 2027, hypothetical replay on a future design). The spec requires the disclaimer; the wording should state plainly that in September the team replays a May session on the target design.

results.quote: its main geo query is a radius around the buyer's postcode in German (*Umkreissuche*)
results.finding: Both readers first read this as the postcode being in German; it means the query is called Umkreissuche in German.

results.quote: Elasticsearch documents these primitives, and OpenSearch uses the same names
results.finding: Reader A only: the engine-documentation paragraph sits between the definitions and 'Three semantic traps sit inside the table', so the table is two paragraphs back when the traps refer to it; its vertex-cost point is used only in Drawn Polygons. The order (p12 before p13) is the spec's.

results.quote: As the table below shows, only real estate is map-first; jobs use commute, rarely the map.
results.finding: Reader A only: the prose summarizes a table the reader has not yet seen and then covers Motorvane, Elasticsearch and local liquidity before the table appears.

results.quote: Motorvane stays on Elasticsearch until a 2029 review, which does not stop it using the shared geo query compiler: the geo primitives in this chapter exist in both engines.
results.finding: Reader B only: a platform-migration note inside a paragraph comparing how place matters by vertical reads as out of place. The spec's p50 controlling idea requires this note here.

Every does_not_know term is defined at first use: bounding box, map tile and isochrone (Five Ways ¶2), zoom/x/y tiles and geotile_grid (Architecture ¶5), geo clustering (Clustering ¶1), vector tiles (clustering table and _mvt sources), geo_point/geo_shape and tessellation (Five Ways ¶3), Douglas-Peucker simplification (Drawn Polygons ¶2), travel-time matrices (commute table; 'per element of a matrix'), routing commercial terms (Commute ¶4), Valhalla and GTFS (Commute ¶5). NDCG, BKD tree, DPE and percolation are glossed. Common Ground and Motorvane, which both flow readers queried (A items 10, 12; B items 11, 12), are on audience.already_knows (Veldmark's brands and the Common Ground program), so they are not failures for this audience.

The opening bridges from recommendations and states a disputable position ('for many listing marketplaces that is backwards') with concrete buyer examples; no dictionary opening, throat-clearing or generic-context pattern.
The conclusion is not a section-by-section recap or a new-topic tease: it gives one answer to the three questions, names consequences and hands off with a stated reason.

From Maps to Standing Promises ¶1 joins the claims into 'the server owns place' and shows that one component settles speed, privacy, duplicates and routing cost; the so-what (moving Hearthly onto the shared platform without The Forced Fit, adding new place interfaces without rebuilding geo logic per client) matches the spec.

The conclusion answers 'Ingrid's three questions' and names the 1.8-second polygons and Agence Rhône Habitat's flat as one pin; the per-request quote is recalled only implicitly ('routing is bought on a forecast of peak volumes'), which is enough for the callback.

The cold reader's predicted order (case and three questions, five ways, map as different product, compiler, then polygons, clustering, commute, neighborhood data, peak performance, Lyon walk-through, trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, CA view, questions) matches the roadmap promises in order, and the evidence kinds match. Its open points (the three questions not stated in the opening, neighborhood data unexplained) are answered by the scene and the body and do not contradict the roadmap.

The cold reader of the opening alone lists every section in the expected order and the four kinds of evidence (Airbnb and Zillow, Rightmove case studies, engine and routing documentation, fictional Veldmark/Hearthly). It cannot state the three questions or that Lyon is the polygon problem's location, which the expected answer names only at the level the opening gives.

The cold answer matches the expected design: a server-side geo query compiler in front of the engine that repairs, simplifies and caps drawn polygons, snaps viewports to tiles and turns named areas into place-ID filters; pins and clusters from the public point and counted per canonical property so the flat is one pin with three offers; commute as cached isochrones keyed by a snapped H3 origin plus travel-time matrices for pins on screen; routing chosen from a forecast of peak isochrone and matrix volumes against pricing, limits and storage/display terms, with per-request cost rising with campaigns and a fixed license or self-hosted engine turning it into capacity planning. Ownership by the search platform is implied ('the server should own place') rather than stated.

The cold answer names the leak (cluster of one at high zoom, fine heatmaps and vector-tile hits computed from the exact point reveal the seller's front door) and the rule: all returned geometry from a deterministic public point (snapped cell center or seeded offset, so averaging cannot reveal the true point), the map search API unable to read the exact point, minimum counts per cell for area statistics, and a platform invariant signed off by the DPO. Matches expected.

The cold answer explains that map attention follows geography not position, that the map shows every match as pins or clusters so ranking moves to which pins to show, highlight and list, cites Airbnb's 2024 paper and the 2025 review (about 80% of search interactions, list NDCG fails on maps), states that applying this to portals is the author's inference with no published portal evidence, and proposes contacts and saves per map session and time to shortlist. Matches expected.
